title: Mount Hiei
hookLine: Saicho founds Tendai on Mount Hiei, the mountain where later founders trained

cards: A young monk, newly ordained, leaves the great temples of Nara behind and climbs a forested mountain to the northeast of where Kyoto now stands. He builds a small hall and sits in it.
He isn't trying to start anything grand. He wants quiet, the sutras, and time. But the hut grows.

Students come, then more halls, then a whole monastic world among the cedars. Generations later, monks trained on that slope will come down and start schools of their own. The young monk's name is Saicho.

teach.b: Saicho traveled to China and studied the Tiantai teaching, one of the Chinese schools met earlier, built around the Lotus Sutra. Back in Japan he founded it on Mount Hiei, where it took the name Tendai.
Tendai held a wide range under one roof: study of the Lotus Sutra, meditation, the monastic precepts and esoteric ritual. Saicho wrote demanding rules for his students.
He asks them to stay on the mountain for twelve years without going down, studying and practicing the whole time.

In the same writings he says that a person who lights up one corner of the world is a treasure of the nation. Not a well-known person, not a powerful one. Someone who brightens the corner they're standing in.

Tradition remembers several later founders of Japanese schools as having trained on Mount Hiei before going their own way: Honen and Shinran, who taught the Pure Land path; Dogen, who brought a Zen lineage home from China; Nichiren, who centered everything on the Lotus Sutra.
They taught very differently, and this path will reach their stories.

teach.h: A SLOPE IN YOUR OWN STORY.
teach.b: But they learned their first lessons on the same slope.
And one face from a few days back: Ennin, who watched the persecution of 845 with his diary in hand, was Saicho's student, and returned to lead the mountain.
There may be a slope like this in your own story: a kitchen, a workshop, a classroom, a team, where you learned the basics before going your own way.

how: Mount Hiei is still the head center of the Tendai school, where monks train in study, meditation and ritual, and Saicho is honored by Tendai Buddhists as Dengyo Daishi.

games.q: you're Saicho, writing rules for your students on the mountain. how long do you ask them to stay?
o: as long as each one likes.
games.why: his rules ask for twelve years on the mountain, studying and practicing the whole time.

practice: Bring to mind the place where you first learned something that still shapes you, a family table, a gym, a temple or church hall, a first job, and see its light and its people.
Remember one teacher there, named or unnamed, and if you'd like, thank that place silently in a few plain words.

wordCard.voice: Mount Hiei. The mountain where Saicho founded Tendai, wrote his rules for long training, and where later founders of Japanese schools first learned.
